title: Quantum geometry of collective pairing fluctuations in the superfluid weight of multiband superconductors
abstract: Beyond the frozen-pairing contribution, the superfluid weight of a multiband superconductor contains a correction from the self-consistent relaxation of the pairing amplitudes under a phase twist. We show that this correction has a quantum-geometric origin, not in the space of Bloch states but in the space of collective pairing fields. For an attractive multiband Hubbard model at the mean-field level, the thermodynamic Hessian governing the pairing response coincides with the static Gaussian pair-fluctuation kernel at zero momentum at every temperature below $T_c$. Since gauge invariance relates a phase twist to a finite center-of-mass momentum of the pair field, the superfluid weight is set by the small-momentum curvature of the eigenvalue branch that evolves from the Goldstone mode, and the relaxation correction is a stiffness-weighted quantum metric of the corresponding soft eigenvector on the manifold of pairing configurations. The same construction yields the Ginzburg-Landau gradient coefficient with the identical geometric correction, hence the coherence-length tensor, and, with the low-frequency dynamics of the kernel, the pair-mass tensor. Lieb-lattice calculations verify the equivalence of the thermodynamic, fluctuation-kernel, and soft-mode formulations and the independence of the superfluid weight from the orbital embedding.
summary: This theoretical work derives the superfluid weight for multiband superconductors by identifying a quantum-geometric correction stemming from pairing fluctuations. It rigorously proves the equivalence between thermodynamic calculations and those derived from the effective action, showing that the superfluid weight is dictated by the curvature of the pairing field manifold. This provides a deep, geometric understanding of superconducting response properties.
main_problem: The paper determines the superfluid weight of multiband superconductors, focusing on a quantum-geometric correction arising from the self-consistent relaxation of pairing amplitudes under a phase twist.
main_result: The superfluid weight is shown to be determined by the small-momentum curvature of the eigenvalue branch evolving from the Goldstone mode, and this geometric correction is equivalent to the Ginzburg-Landau gradient coefficient.
method: The analysis uses a combination of thermodynamic potential minimization (saddle-point equations) and effective action formalism to calculate the curvature of the pairing response along the self-consistent solution.
model_or_system: The system is a multiband superconductor modeled using an attractive multiband Hubbard model. The analysis is performed at the mean-field level, considering the pairing field $\Psi$ and its response to a phase twist $q$.
key_observables: Superfluid weight tensor ($V_{Ds}$), Ginzburg-Landau gradient coefficient (coherence-length tensor), and the pair-mass tensor.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), phase twist momentum ($q$), and the Hubbard interaction strength ($U$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed at the mean-field level, and the derivation relies on the assumption that gauge invariance relates a phase twist to a finite center-of-mass momentum.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the superfluid weight calculated using three different methods, confirming their agreement and demonstrating the cancellation of spurious terms in the disconnected limit.
paper_structure: The paper develops the calculation by first defining the thermodynamic potential $\Omega_0(q, \Delta, \Delta^*)$ and finding the self-consistent solution $\Delta_0(q)$. It then derives the superfluid weight from the curvature of $\Omega(q)$, comparing this result to calculations based on the effective action and fluctuation kernel, and finally proving the equivalence of these formulations.
why_interesting: The geometric interpretation of the superfluid weight, linking it to the curvature of the pairing manifold, provides a powerful, universal framework for understanding superconducting response beyond simple mean-field treatments.
